topic: Manual gearbox synchro: why doesn't it grind when you change gear? (the brass synchronizer ring rubs the gear's cone until the gear spins at shaft speed, and only then lets the sleeve lock the gear to the shaft).
principle: The selected gear spins freely on the output shaft (driven by the countershaft) while the sleeve turns with the shaft on a hub fixed to it; shifting slides the sleeve, which presses the brass synchronizer ring onto the gear's cone, cone friction brings the gear to shaft speed while the ring (twisted slightly by that friction) blocks the sleeve, and once the speeds match the ring turns back in line and the sleeve slides through it onto the gear's dog teeth, locking gear and shaft together without grinding.

firstComment:
Answer: brass 🔧 It's the synchronizer ring (synchro).

In a manual gearbox the gears are always in mesh. The gear you want spins freely on the output shaft, often at a different speed than the shaft. The sleeve turns with the shaft, so if it slammed straight into the gear's dog teeth, they would clash and grind.

When you move the lever, the fork slides the sleeve. First it presses the brass ring onto a cone on the gear. Friction brings the gear to the same speed as the shaft (watch the two yellow marks line up). While the speeds are still different, the ring is twisted slightly and blocks the sleeve.

Once the speeds match, the ring turns back in line, the sleeve slides through it onto the gear's dog teeth, and the gear is locked to the shaft. No grinding.

(Simplified 3D model: one gear and one synchro, straight-cut teeth, the clutch is pressed. Real gearboxes use helical gears and pointed teeth on the sleeve and ring.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Manual transmission (when the dog clutches are disengaged all gears spin freely around the output shaft; the selector is splined to the shaft and moved by a fork linked to the gear lever; without matched speeds the dog teeth fail to engage and grind; brass synchronizer rings use cone friction to equalize speeds; blocker rings twist slightly from the cone's friction torque and prevent engagement until the speeds are synchronized): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manual_transmission
Lesics, Manual transmission, how it works? (output gears loosely connected to the shaft; hub fixed to the shaft with a sliding sleeve; the sleeve presses the synchronizer ring against the cone, friction makes the gear speed the same as the shaft, then the sleeve slides in and locks the gear): https://lesics.com/manual-transmission-how-it-works.html
altText: 3D animation of a manual gearbox synchro. A silver gearbox case with a black gear knob sits on a gray studio backdrop under the question Why doesn't it grind? A red circle marks the knob. The case fades away to show a steel output shaft with a large gear driven by a smaller gear on the shaft below. Next to the gear sit an orange brass ring and a polished sleeve held by a dark fork. A yellow mark on the gear and a yellow stripe on the sleeve show the gear spinning faster than the shaft. The fork pushes the sleeve, which presses the brass ring onto a cone on the gear; the gear slows until the two yellow marks line up and move together. Then the sleeve slides over the ring onto the gear's teeth and locks it to the shaft. The sleeve moves back, the case fades back in and the video loops. Text on screen: Why doesn't it grind? Gear spins faster. Ring rubs the cone. Speeds match. Sleeve slides in. Locked. No grind. Follow, new machine tomorrow.
